subject: General Knowledge
topic: Indian music & musical instruments — mixed tiers

questions.stem: Pandit Shivkumar Sharma is the foremost exponent of which instrument that also forms the backbone of traditional Kashmiri Sufiana Kalam music?

options.option_text: Sarangi — a bowed short-necked lute of Hindustani music
Santoor — a hammered dulcimer that originated in Kashmir
Rudra Veena — an ancient plucked string instrument of Dhrupad
Pakhawaj — a barrel-shaped drum used in Dhrupad performances

questions.explanation: The Santoor is correct. Shivkumar Sharma almost single-handedly elevated the Santoor from a Kashmiri folk instrument (used in Sufiana Kalam devotional music) into a Hindustani classical concert instrument. The Rudra Veena (Option C) is tempting because it is also an ancient string instrument, but it belongs to the Dhrupad tradition and is associated with the Dagarvani gharana, not with Kashmir.

questions.stem: In Bharata Muni's 'Natyashastra' fourfold classification, instruments such as the Venu (flute) and Shankha (conch) are grouped under which category?

options.option_text: Tata Vadya — instruments that produce sound via stretched strings
Ghana Vadya — solid instruments that vibrate to produce their sound
Avanaddha Vadya — instruments fitted with a taut vibrating membrane
Sushira Vadya — hollow wind instruments blown to produce sound

questions.explanation: Sushira Vadya (hollow/air-column instruments) is correct; the flute and conch both produce sound through blown air in a hollow cavity. Avanaddha Vadya (Option C) covers membrane instruments like Tabla and Mridangam, which is the most common distractor because both categories are wind- or breath-associated in everyday thinking. The four Natyashastra categories — Tata, Sushira, Avanaddha, Ghana — map roughly to chordophone, aerophone, membranophone, and idiophone.

questions.stem: The Pakhawaj barrel drum is the traditional percussion accompaniment for which Hindustani genre, setting it apart from the Tabla-dominated Khyal tradition?

options.option_text: Thumri — a semi-classical romantic vocal genre of North India
Dhrupad — the oldest surviving form of Hindustani classical music
Tappa — a semi-classical genre originating from Punjab camel drivers
Dadra — a light classical vocal form set in six-beat tala cycles

questions.explanation: Dhrupad is correct. The Pakhawaj (also called Mardala or Pushkar) is the dedicated accompaniment for Dhrupad, the most austere and oldest surviving Hindustani form. When Khyal gradually displaced Dhrupad from the 18th century, the Tabla replaced the Pakhawaj in mainstream performance. Thumri (Option A) is a frequent distractor because it is also a traditional vocal genre, but it uses the Tabla.

questions.stem: The 'Khamak', a one-sided drum with a gut string attached to the membrane that is plucked rather than struck, is most closely associated with the folk tradition of which Indian state?

options.option_text: Rajasthan — home of the Manganiyar and Langa musical communities
West Bengal — integral to the mystic Baul folk music tradition
Punjab — associated with the Bhangra and Giddha folk traditions
Assam — linked to Bihu celebrations and the Dhol-Pepa tradition

questions.explanation: West Bengal is correct. The Khamak (also called Gubguba or Anandalahari) is iconic to Baul mystic singers of Bengal; the player plucks the string while pressing the membrane to bend pitch, producing its characteristic twanging sound. Rajasthan (Option A) is a plausible distractor because it is India's most recognised folk-music state, but Rajasthani folk instruments include the Ravanhatta, Morchang, and Algoza — not the Khamak.

questions.stem: The Saraswati Veena, widely regarded as India's national instrument, was awarded a Geographical Indication (GI) tag for its traditional craftsmanship concentrated in which city?

options.option_text: Mysuru — famous for its silk sarees and sandalwood carvings
Chennai — the nerve centre of Carnatic music concerts and academies
Thanjavur — the historic seat of Saraswati Veena luthiery in Tamil Nadu
Tiruchirapalli — home to the Srirangam temple and Carnatic music

questions.explanation: Thanjavur is correct. The Thanjavur Veena (Saraswati Veena) received its GI tag due to its centuries-old craft cluster in Thanjavur district. Its distinctive feature is a single hollowed-out jackwood body with an integral resonator, unlike the Mysuru style. Chennai (Option B) is a tempting distractor because it is the cultural capital of Carnatic music, but the craft of making the veena is Thanjavur-centred, not Chennai-centred.

questions.stem: The Chitraveena (Gottuvadyam) is set apart from the Saraswati Veena primarily by which structural and playing-technique feature?

options.option_text: It has 21 strings in triple courses, broadly similar to a Sitar's layout
It is entirely fretless and played with a cylindrical glass or stone slide
It uses a horsehair bow instead of finger-plucking for tone production
It has a double-chambered gourd resonator to enhance bass frequencies

questions.explanation: Fretless slide technique is correct. The Chitraveena has no frets whatsoever; the player rests a smooth cylindrical object (kammalam) made of glass or polished stone on the strings to slide across pitches, enabling microtonal gamaka ornaments impossible on a fretted Saraswati Veena. N. Ravikiran is the foremost living exponent. Option C (horsehair bow) describes the Sarangi or Dilruba — bowed instruments — and is a classic confusion because both produce continuous tones.

questions.stem: The Nadaswaram (Nagasvaram), one of the loudest non-brass acoustic wind instruments in the world, is by South Indian tradition exclusively performed at which type of occasion?

options.option_text: Carnatic classical stage concerts performed in sabhas and auditoriums
Harvest and seasonal festivals such as Pongal and Vishu celebrations
Temple rituals, wedding processions, and other auspicious ceremonies
Devotional bhajan and kirtan sessions held in Vaishnavite temples

questions.explanation: Temple rituals and auspicious ceremonies are correct. The Nadaswaram is classified as a mangala vadyam (auspicious instrument) and its performance is traditionally inseparable from weddings, temple processions, and religious rites in Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh. It is NOT performed in classical sabha concerts (Option A) — that role belongs to the Flute or Veena. Option B is a distractor because Pongal and Vishu are common knowledge, but Nadaswaram's context is the sacred/auspicious ritual setting, not seasonal festivals per se.
